questions.prompt: What is the primary defense against SQL Injection vulnerabilities in backend database queries?
options: Parameterized queries / Prepared statements with parameterized arguments
Encoding user input with base64 before inserting into the query string
Using HTTP POST instead of GET
Restricting database connection strings to localhost
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries separate the SQL command code from user data, ensuring input is treated as literal parameter values rather than executable syntax.

questions.prompt: How does Stored Cross-Site Scripting (Stored XSS) differ from Reflected XSS?
options: Stored XSS is permanently saved in the database or server storage and delivered to every user requesting that page; Reflected XSS requires the payload to be delivered in the immediate request (e.g. search query parameter)
Reflected XSS only affects mobile applications
Stored XSS cannot steal authentication tokens
Reflected XSS requires administrative server access
questions.explanation: Stored XSS persists on the backend (e.g. forum post or profile comment), executing whenever victims load the stored content.

questions.prompt: What HTTP response header instructs modern browsers to restrict resources (scripts, styles, images) to trusted origins, mitigating XSS?
options: Content-Security-Policy (CSP)
X-Frame-Options
Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS)
Access-Control-Allow-Origin
questions.explanation: Content-Security-Policy defines trusted sources for script execution, blocking inline script injections and unauthorized domains.

questions.prompt: In penetration testing, what is the objective of the Reconnaissance / OSINT phase?
options: Gathering passive and active intelligence about the target organization (subdomains, open ports, employee emails, tech stack) before active exploitation
Deploying ransomware immediately
Formatting all hard drives on the target
Installing keyloggers on the CEO workstation
questions.explanation: Reconnaissance gathers target infrastructure intelligence to map the attack surface and identify potential attack vectors.

questions.prompt: What is a SYN Stealth Scan (`nmap -sS`) and why is it frequently used?
options: It sends a TCP SYN packet and teardowns the connection with RST upon receiving SYN-ACK without completing the 3-way handshake, avoiding application-level logging
It connects via SSH and runs system diagnostics
It scans over UDP exclusively
It automatically cracks root passwords
questions.explanation: SYN scanning probes open ports by sending RST immediately upon receiving SYN-ACK, never completing the full TCP handshake.

questions.prompt: What vulnerability allows an attacker to manipulate server-side code into making arbitrary HTTP requests to internal, non-routable services (e.g. AWS metadata `169.254.169.254`)?
options: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR)
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) misconfiguration
questions.explanation: SSRF tricks the backend server into sending requests to loopback addresses or internal microservices inaccessible from the public internet.

questions.prompt: What is Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR / BOLA)?
options: An application exposes a direct database key or identifier in a request without validating that the authenticated user possesses authorization to access that object
Using public Wi-Fi without a VPN
Storing passwords using MD5
Running unencrypted HTTP on port 80
questions.explanation: IDOR occurs when an API accepts an object ID (e.g. GET /api/invoice/456) without enforcing that user 123 owns invoice 456.

questions.prompt: Why should password hashing algorithms like Argon2id or bcrypt be used instead of fast cryptographic hashes like SHA-256 or SHA-512?
options: Argon2 and bcrypt have configurable work factors (cost) and memory requirements designed to be computationally expensive, neutralizing GPU and ASIC brute-force attacks
SHA-256 is deprecated and cannot hash strings over 10 characters
bcrypt hashes are completely reversible by administrators
SHA-512 does not support salting
questions.explanation: Fast hashes allow billions of guesses per second on consumer GPUs; slow, memory-hard key derivation functions (KDFs) make offline cracking intractable.

questions.prompt: What is a 'Reverse Shell'?
options: A connection where the compromised target machine initiates an outbound network connection back to the attacker's listening machine, bypassing inbound firewall rules
An attacker connecting directly to the victim's SSH port
A shell script written in reverse alphabetical order
A hardware dongle plugged into the USB port
questions.explanation: Outbound egress traffic is frequently permitted by corporate firewalls, allowing reverse shells to establish interactive command sessions where inbound connections would be blocked.

questions.prompt: What is Privilege Escalation in ethical hacking?
options: Exploiting design flaws or software bugs to gain higher level access (e.g. root/administrator) from an initially compromised low-privileged account
Promoting an employee to an executive role
Increasing the memory allocation of a virtual machine
Bypassing MFA during legitimate user login
questions.explanation: Vertical privilege escalation involves advancing privileges from a standard user to root/SYSTEM by exploiting misconfigurations, SUID binaries, or kernel flaws.

questions.prompt: What does the `SameSite=Strict` cookie attribute enforce?
options: The browser never sends the cookie in cross-site requests, providing robust protection against CSRF
The cookie can only be read over HTTPS
The cookie expires after 10 minutes
JavaScript can read the cookie from any origin
questions.explanation: SameSite=Strict ensures the cookie is withheld on cross-site requests (including standard incoming links), preventing CSRF.

questions.prompt: What is an XML External Entity (XXE) injection attack?
options: Attacking an application that parses XML input where external entity references are resolved, enabling arbitrary local file disclosure or SSRF
Injecting SQL statements into HTML tags
Overwriting JSON schema definitions
Flooding XML web services with UDP traffic
questions.explanation: XXE exploits weakly configured XML parsers that expand external entity definitions (e.g. <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM 'file:///etc/passwd'>).

questions.prompt: What is the difference between asymmetric and symmetric cryptography?
options: Symmetric uses the same secret key for encryption and decryption; Asymmetric uses a mathematically linked public-private key pair
Asymmetric uses a single key; Symmetric uses two keys
Symmetric is only used for digital signatures
Asymmetric is 1,000 times faster than symmetric algorithms
questions.explanation: Symmetric algorithms (e.g. AES) use a shared secret; asymmetric algorithms (e.g. RSA, ECC) use public keys for encryption/verification and private keys for decryption/signing.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security)?
options: Informs browsers that the site must only be accessed over HTTPS, preventing SSL stripping and downgrade attacks
Compresses HTTP body payloads
Caches static assets in browser memory
Restricts access by geographic IP range
questions.explanation: HSTS header forces user-agents to automatically convert all http:// links to https:// before sending network requests.

questions.prompt: What is a 'Pass-the-Hash' (PtH) attack in an Active Directory environment?
options: An attacker uses an extracted NTLM password hash directly to authenticate to remote services without needing to crack or know the plain text password
Sending MD5 hashes in HTTP request headers
Modifying cryptographic salts in the database
Brute forcing Kerberos ticket expiration dates
questions.explanation: Because Windows NTLM authentication protocol proves identity using the password hash directly, possessing the hash is sufficient to authenticate across the domain.

questions.prompt: What is Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) intended to do?
options: Allow web servers to explicitly declare which foreign origins are permitted to read its responses, relaxing the browser's default Same-Origin Policy
Prevent server-side SQL injection
Block search engines from indexing pages
Encrypt database backups
questions.explanation: CORS is a browser security mechanism that enables servers to selectively authorize cross-origin HTTP requests.

questions.prompt: Which tool is standard for intercepting, modifying, and inspecting web application HTTP traffic during security testing?
options: Burp Suite / OWASP ZAP
Wireshark exclusively
Metasploit
Vim
questions.explanation: Burp Suite and OWASP ZAP act as local HTTP intercepting proxies allowing detailed inspection and manipulation of web requests.

questions.prompt: What is Mass Assignment vulnerability?
options: Binding client-provided HTTP request parameters directly into database model instances without filtering, allowing attackers to overwrite protected fields like `is_admin`
Assigning tasks to multiple security analysts simultaneously
Sending emails to 10,000 recipients at once
Running multiple unit tests in parallel
questions.explanation: Mass assignment occurs when ORM frameworks blindly bind all JSON properties to entity models, allowing attackers to set privileged attributes.

questions.prompt: In public key infrastructure, what does Certificate Transparency (CT) provide?
options: An open public framework of append-only cryptographic log servers that monitor and audit TLS certificate issuance to detect rogue or fraudulent certificates
A method to disclose private keys to law enforcement
A way to bypass HTTPS warning screens
A protocol to encrypt DNS queries
questions.explanation: Certificate Transparency logs ensure that domain owners can audit which certificate authorities have issued certificates for their domain.

questions.prompt: Why should sensitive credentials never be stored directly in Git repositories?
options: Git commit history permanently retains secrets even if the file is modified or removed in later commits, exposing them to anyone with repository access
Git encrypts all repositories automatically
Credentials slow down git pull speed
Git repositories reject files with API keys
questions.explanation: Git commits are immutable snapshots; secrets remain in git history and packfiles indefinitely unless purged with rewriting tools like git-filter-repo.

codingTasks.prompt: Write a function `sanitizeHtml(rawString)` that escapes dangerous HTML characters (`&`, `<`, `>`, `"`, `'`) to their corresponding HTML entities to prevent Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).

hiddenTests.input: const { sanitizeHtml } = require('./solution'); console.log(sanitizeHtml(''));

codingTasks.prompt: Write a function `validatePasswordStrength(password)` that validates password complexity: minimum 8 characters, at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one digit, and one special character (any of `!@#$%^&*`). Return `{ valid: boolean, errors: string[] }`.

Write a function `isPathTraversal(pathString)` that inspects a requested relative filepath and returns `true` if it attempts directory traversal (e.g. contains `..`, URL-encoded `%2e%2e`, or backslashes escaping boundaries), or `false` if it is a safe local filename.

Write a function `maskSensitiveData(record, sensitiveKeys)` that takes an object and returns a shallow copy where values for any keys in `sensitiveKeys` are masked with `'***REDACTED***'`. If a key does not exist, ignore it.

hiddenTests.input: const { maskSensitiveData } = require('./solution'); const orig = { k: 'secret' }; maskSensitiveData(orig, ['k']); console.log(orig.k);
const { maskSensitiveData } = require('./solution'); console.log(maskSensitiveData({ p: 'pwd', t: 'tok' }, ['p', 't']).p);
const { maskSensitiveData } = require('./solution'); console.log(maskSensitiveData({ a: null }, ['a']).a);

sqlTasks.prompt: Given table `security_audit_logs(id, user_id, action, ip_address, status, created_at)`, write a query to find IP addresses that have caused more than 3 'failed_login' events in the last 24 hours.
sqlTasks.starterCode:
-- Write SQL query here
SELECT ip_address, COUNT(*) AS failure_count
FROM security_audit_logs
...

visibleTests.input: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM security_audit_logs WHERE status='failed_login';

hiddenTests.input: SELECT ip_address FROM security_audit_logs WHERE status='failed_login' GROUP BY ip_address HAVING count(*) > 3 LIMIT 1;
SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT ip_address FROM security_audit_logs WHERE status='failed_login' GROUP BY ip_address HAVING count(*) > 3);

sqlTasks.prompt: Given table `user_privileges(id, user_id, role, granted_at)`, write a query to list all user_ids who possess more than 1 distinct administrative role.
sqlTasks.starterCode:
-- Write SQL query here
SELECT user_id, COUNT(DISTINCT role) AS admin_roles
FROM user_privileges
...

hiddenTests.input: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT user_id FROM user_privileges GROUP BY user_id HAVING count(DISTINCT role) > 1);

projects.prompt:
Mini-Project: Web Application Vulnerability Remediation & Hardening Plan.
Review a vulnerable Node.js/Express endpoint and implement security defenses:
1. Fix SQL Injection using parameterized queries.
2. Remediate Reflected XSS with output encoding.
3. Implement Helmet security headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options).
4. Add IP-based rate limiting on sensitive auth endpoints.
5. Enforce strong session cookie configurations (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict).

rubric.label: Vulnerability Remediation
rubric.description: Eliminates SQL injection and XSS through parameterized inputs and contextual output sanitization.

rubric.label: Security Headers & CSP
rubric.description: Correctly configures strict Content-Security-Policy, HSTS, and X-Content-Type-Options.

rubric.label: Session & Cookie Hardening
rubric.description: Proper cookie flags (HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Secure) and credential protection.

rubric.label: Brute Force & Rate Limiting
rubric.description: Implements robust request rate limiting to deter automated credential stuffing.
